extracted.intended_audience: student journalists / high-school and college journalism students
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for writing feature/box stories and human-interest interviews, emphasizing unity, tone, economy of wording, interview technique, and story organization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three required elements of a feature story
rubrics_metrics.description: Unity, dominant tone, totality of effect (single effect).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A feature must be unified and coherent; state the unified effect in one word (wetness, sympathy, mild amusement, bewilderment, etc.). Analyze what is emphasized and how unity, dominant tone, and totality of effect are achieved. The short feature contains exactly the same elements as the longer feature article.

rubrics_metrics.name: Box story characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Any short item—news, schedule, special announcement or feature—suitable to be set in a box to catch the eye and lend grace to page make-up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Box stories are brief items enclosed in a rectangle, usually placed at the top of the page to give variety to top headlines. Very short feature stories make the most attractive boxes; condense novel or colorful material into box size.

rubrics_metrics.name: Box story terseness and clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: The box story must be terse, stripped of all unnecessary words, and have no awkward or obscure phrasing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short features for boxes should be concise yet clear—terse wording without obscurity or awkward phrasing. They should still achieve unity and a single dominant effect despite brevity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choosing subjects for human-interest interviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Persons of importance; persons of influence; the first to attempt a thing; the first to succeed; the expert; champions; the unique; one who has achieved distinction in any field; anyone who can tell of the new, the strange, the picturesque, the unexpected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select interview subjects who offer personality and/or novelty that will engage readers and produce colorful, informative copy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparation before the interview
rubrics_metrics.description: Get the history of the person to be interviewed and the history of the subject; prepare questions for the interview.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Researching background and preparing questions helps recall and ensures coverage of important facts; preparation improves the chance of obtaining quotable, newsworthy material.

rubrics_metrics.name: During the interview — recording what matters
rubrics_metrics.description: Note significant phrases for quotation; note words, phrases, or sentences peculiarly characteristic of the person; note personality, mannerisms, setting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct quotation gives life to a narrative. Record gestures, voice, movement and facial expression. Be alive to chance hints or remarks that have news value. If the person drifts into picturesque material, allow it up to a point—it may enrich the article.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct of the interviewer
rubrics_metrics.description: Be insistent but courteous; if you want an opinion get it by tactfully leading the conversation into suitable channels; don't break into what may prove far more picturesque and colorful to your article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance persistence with courtesy; use tactful prompting rather than interruption to obtain opinions or steer the subject without squelching spontaneous colorful material.

rubrics_metrics.name: After the interview — immediate review and synthesis
rubrics_metrics.description: Jot down impressions at once lest any significant details be lost; have more than you can use; make a brief review and judge what was most significant; put it into the lead when you begin to write.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Immediate notes preserve fresh impressions. Select the facts or quotes that best summarize the conversation and craft the lead around them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organization plan of an interview story
rubrics_metrics.description: Include setting early in the article and stage business to inject the personality of the person interviewed (voice, gesture, movement, facial expression).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use setting and 'stage business' to make the subject 'live and breathe' for the reader; suit the stage business to the words and use it to illustrate character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cautions in interview writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Suit the action to the word, not the word to the action; don't mix direct and indirect discourse in the same paragraph; keep the person interviewed in the mind of your readers by referring to him; don't use 'said' too often.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Find appropriate epithets and synonyms for 'said'; where possible absorb stage business into the verb (e.g., instead of 'he said in a decisive tone,' write 'he cut in'). Maintain clarity by avoiding mixing quotation styles in a paragraph.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topic and technique suggestions for feature stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Animals, incongruity, seasonal events and novelty are fruitful bases for features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Animals make interesting subject-matter; incongruity is frequently the basis of humorous features; feature stories often come out with the season—write seasonal pieces (Christmas, first snow, etc.) and play up striking local details or machines to justify placement in the paper.
